weaknesses: The paper's headline practical claim — that the finite programs make the minimax value auditable — is never reconciled with the sizes it itself reports. Section 5 opens "This section makes that scale numerically accessible" and the discussion lists the certificates as one of "three complementary checks" a designer can run, yet the only quantitative size statement is the orbit-counts clause of \cref{obj:thm:rational-contrast-grid-certificate-sandwich}: the LP has |M_{n,K}| = binom(n+2^K-1, 2^K-1) risk rows and binom(n+2K-1,2K-1)(2M+1) grid variables, which at the prescribed mesh M=n is already astronomically large for K=3 and n in the tens. Fix: replace the "numerically accessible" framing in the first paragraph of Section 5 with an explicit dimension count as a function of (n,K,M), state the range of n at which the program is actually solvable, and reframe the contribution in the discussion as an exact finite characterization with a mesh-controlled bracket rather than a design-practice audit.

No instance of the certificate programs is ever solved, so the reader cannot tell whether the second-order bracket is informative. The certified envelope is [C_0(c)\kappa_c, 43 C_0(c)] with \kappa_c = (1/2)min{\sqrt{\lambda_c}/2 - \lambda_c/16, 7\lambda_c/16}, which for the paper's own diagnostic contrast c^\dagger is a two-orders-of-magnitude window, and \kappa_c degenerates linearly as \lambda_c \to 0. Fix: add a short paragraph after \cref{obj:thm:universal-second-order-rate} that evaluates \lambda_c and \kappa_c for c=(1,-1) and c^\dagger, states the resulting numeric ratio between the two constants, and says plainly that the sharp constant is open (currently this is only alluded to obliquely in the boundary-layer remark).

The relation to the sharp two-arm literature is asserted but never made precise, and the paper's own two-arm input is coarse. Related work says \citet{sudijono_dobriban_tchetgen_2026_sharp} "obtains a sharp two-arm binary expansion", yet \cref{obj:thm:coarse-two-arm-minimax-lower} proves a self-contained bound with constant 43 that then propagates into every multi-arm statement. Fix: in Related work and again in the paragraph following \cref{obj:thm:coarse-two-arm-minimax-lower}, state with a theorem locator exactly what the cited two-arm result establishes, say why a self-contained coarse converse is proved instead, and state what the multi-arm constant would become if the sharp two-arm constant were imported.

The paper does not delimit which conclusions are genuinely multi-arm. For |S_c| = 2, \cref{obj:thm:embedded-two-arm-converse} and \cref{obj:thm:attainment-and-k3-certified-converse} show \rho_n(c) = C_0(c)\rho_{n,2}, i.e. the problem is exactly two-arm after rescaling; for |S_c| \ge 3, what is delivered is an order bound plus existence of finite programs. Fix: add a paragraph at the end of the introduction, or opening Section 6, that separates the conclusions inherited from two arms (the value for |S_c|=2, the 43 C_0 converse) from the ones that are new at |S_c| \ge 3 (the orbit reduction, the \lambda_c-dependent shrinkage constant, the scalar-score separation).

The ACTG 175 framing is decorative and the three-arm scalar-score proposition is oversold. The trial is invoked twice ("multi-regimen binary-endpoint trials, including ACTG 175-style comparisons among zidovudine monotherapy, ...") without any of its contrasts being worked through, and \cref{obj:prop:k3-scalar-score-not-minimax-preserving} — a single n=3 comparison under the fixed design D^\star against one particular signed-score reduction — is generalized in the discussion to "collapsing observations to a scalar sign score can change the minimax value". Fix: either compute L_c, q^\star, \lambda_c and C_0 for two named ACTG-175 contrasts or reduce the trial to one illustrative sentence; and qualify both the introduction and discussion sentences to "at n=3 under the contrast-weighted design D^\star".

The estimator class — the single modelling restriction that makes the whole minimax problem well posed — is never motivated or discussed. \cref{obj:def:labeled-schedule-game} writes the infimum over "\widehat\tau" with no stated range, the restriction to [-L_c/2, L_c/2] appears only later in \cref{obj:synth_3} and \cref{obj:synth_14}, and the paper simultaneously calls \rho_n(c) "the unrestricted labeled-schedule minimax risk" throughout. Fix: state the estimator range inside \cref{obj:def:labeled-schedule-game}, add two sentences in the setup explaining that the clipping is the target's own range and is therefore harmless (with the projection argument used in the proofs), and drop or requalify the word "unrestricted", which currently misdescribes the criterion in the abstract, introduction, and every theorem preamble.

Positioning against the closest prior work is too vague to let the reader see what is new. Section 'Related work' says only that Sudijono, Dobriban and Tchetgen "obtains a sharp two-arm binary expansion" and that Hull "studies bounded two-arm potential outcomes". Because the paper's own two-arm input (thm:coarse-two-arm-minimax-lower) is exactly a two-arm second-order lower bound, the reader needs one or two sentences stating what those papers establish for K=2 (in particular whether the n^{-4/3} order or its constant is already available there), with theorem-level citep locators, and then stating precisely which of the present contributions is the multi-arm increment: the orbit reduction, the contrast-weighted first-order constant for general c, the support-two exact reduction, and the finite programs.

The finite-program contribution is argued entirely in the abstract-existence register and is never instantiated. Section 'Finite-program certificates for rational and real contrasts' asserts the programs are "exactly solvable in principle at moderate n and K", but no LP is ever solved and no bracket [B, U] is ever reported for any (n, K, c); the only numbers in the paper come from a hand-built 20-entry estimator table at n=3. Either report one worked bracket (say K=3, c=(1,-1/2,-1/2), n in the single digits, with B, U, the mesh M, and the row count) so the machinery is shown to bind, or reframe the section explicitly as a representation theorem for the finite-n value and delete the solvability-in-practice suggestion.

thm:multiarm-strict-extension bundles genuine content with statements no reader needs, which inflates the apparent contribution and obscures the real one. Clauses such as "These four response types are pairwise distinct and exhaust T_2", "|T_K| = 2^K", the Hull risk-value inclusion (which is trivially satisfied by taking D'=D, as its own proof does), and the domain separation "Y^Hull ⊄ T_K^n" (a statement about real versus binary coordinates) should be demoted to a remark or to the setup prose, leaving the theorem with the two-arm orbit value, the two-arm target formula, and the fixed-K orbit equality. As it stands the strongest clause (the second-order scale) is buried among bookkeeping.

The assumptions are recapitulated but never interpreted or weighed. The discussion subsection 'Design implications' lists the model ("fixes a finite population and fixed K, encodes each unit by binary potential outcomes ... clips estimators to the feasible contrast range, and lets the adversary range over all labeled binary schedules") without saying what each buys or costs: binary outcomes are what make the response-type space finite and the orbit game exact; the fixed prespecified zero-sum c is what makes the contrast-weighted allocation well defined; the adversary over all schedules includes constant schedules, which is what drives the worst case. Add a short paragraph in the setup motivating these three choices and a matching paragraph in the limitations subsection stating the scope affirmatively (which trials the binary fixed-K prespecified-contrast setting covers) instead of leaving the reader to infer the boundary.
